source.title: Career Launchpad: CV, Profiles, Job Search & Interviews

notes.title: CV vs Resume vs Portfolio
notes.text:
Choose the right document

A resume, CV, and portfolio serve different purposes. The job post, industry, and country should guide your choice. Read the employer's wording carefully instead of assuming the terms always mean the same thing.

Resume

A resume is a short, tailored summary designed to win an interview. Early-career candidates usually keep it to one page and highlight the skills, experience, projects, and measurable results most relevant to one role. A marketing graduate might feature an internship campaign and its audience growth.

Curriculum vitae

A CV presents a fuller academic and professional record and may run for several pages. It is common in academic, research, and medical applications, where publications, conferences, grants, and teaching matter. In the UK and Europe, CV is also the usual term for a resume. In India, employers may use both words interchangeably, so follow the job post.

Portfolio

A portfolio proves skills through selected work. Designers, developers, writers, photographers, and video editors can show three to five strong projects, each with a short explanation of the problem, contribution, and result. The portfolio supports a resume or CV rather than replacing every application document.

Decision rule: use a resume for most corporate roles, a detailed CV when a complete academic record is expected, and a portfolio when the quality of your work must be seen.

notes.title: Writing a Strong Resume
notes.text:
Make the first scan count

A resume should help a recruiter understand your fit quickly. Use a simple structure: contact details, a focused summary, relevant skills, experience or internships, projects, and education. Put the strongest evidence in the top half, use one clean font, and list experience in reverse chronological order.

Write action and result bullets

Strong bullets follow a practical formula: action verb, what you did, and the result. Replace vague duties with evidence. Instead of writing 'Responsible for social media,' write 'Grew Instagram followers by 40% in three months through weekly reels.' Numbers such as percentages, time saved, customers served, or projects completed make the contribution easier to judge.

Tailor for the role

Do not send the same resume everywhere. Compare the job description with your experience and include relevant terms naturally when they are accurate. Many employers use an Applicant Tracking System, or ATS, to organise applications and identify role-related keywords. Tailoring helps both the software and the recruiter see the match.

Keep the file readable

Avoid complex tables, decorative graphics, and text embedded in images because they may be misread by an ATS. Use familiar section headings and save as PDF unless the employer asks for another format. For most fresh graduates, one clear page is more effective than several pages of weak or repeated material.

notes.title: Building a LinkedIn Profile
notes.text:
Show a clear professional direction

A LinkedIn profile should help a recruiter understand who you are, what you can do, and what opportunity you want. Use a recent photo with a clear face, simple background, and good lighting. A banner can reinforce your field without distracting from the profile.

Write a useful headline

Do more than write 'Student' or 'Looking for a job.' Combine a target role with relevant skills or value. For example, 'Aspiring Data Analyst | Excel, SQL, Power BI' gives the reader a direction and useful keywords. Keep the promise accurate and easy to scan.

Complete the main sections

Write the About section in three or four short lines: who you are, what you work on, and what you hope to do next. Reuse strong action-and-result bullets in Experience. Add ten to fifteen relevant skills and ask people who have seen your work to endorse the skills they can honestly confirm.

Build a real network

Send connection requests with a short personal note that explains the shared context. Follow organisations and people in your field, then contribute by posting useful work or commenting thoughtfully each week. If you use Open to Work, choose the visibility that fits your situation; a recruiters-only option is available.

A complete profile opens the door, but consistent, respectful participation builds trust.

notes.title: Instagram and Other Platforms
notes.text:
Choose platforms with a purpose

You do not need a professional account everywhere. Select one or two platforms that match the work you want to show and the people you need to reach. LinkedIn supports professional networking and job discovery. GitHub demonstrates code. Behance, Dribbble, and Adobe Portfolio showcase design. Instagram suits creators, personal brands, and visual work.

Build a professional Instagram

A professional bio should state what you do, who you help, and where people can see more. Use the link field for a portfolio, booking page, or current project. Organise posts around a few repeatable themes such as finished work, learning in progress, and results or client outcomes.

Decide whether one account can represent both your personal and professional identity. If the audiences conflict, separate the accounts or keep personal posts private. Consistency matters more than constant posting: use the same professional name, photo, and basic description across platforms.

Review your digital footprint

Search your own name as an employer might. Check public posts, comments, tagged photos, and old profiles. Remove, hide, or update anything that misrepresents your current judgement or professional goals. Also correct outdated contact details and broken portfolio links.

The goal is not to appear everywhere. It is to make the right evidence easy to find on the platform where your target audience already spends time.

notes.title: Searching for Jobs
notes.text:
Create a repeatable search routine

A good job search uses several channels. Search portals such as LinkedIn Jobs, Naukri, Indeed, and Internshala, but also check company career pages. College placement cells, alumni, professional communities, and employee referrals can surface openings before they become widely visible.

Search and filter intelligently

Combine a target job title with a location, experience level, work arrangement, or important skill. Save useful searches and turn on alerts. Read the complete description before applying. A job description is often an ideal profile rather than a rigid checklist; if you meet roughly 60 to 70 percent of the requirements and can learn the rest, a thoughtful application can still be worthwhile.

Network with a specific ask

When contacting an alumnus or employee, keep the message short and personal. Mention the shared connection, show that you researched the role, and ask for insight rather than demanding a referral. A referral can help an application get noticed, but the relationship should be respectful and honest.

Track every application

Use a simple sheet with the company, role, link, application date, contact, status, and follow-up date. Update it immediately after each action. A weekly cycle works well: search for suitable roles, submit tailored applications, follow up where appropriate, and update the tracker.

Tracking turns a stressful search into a process you can review and improve.

notes.title: Giving a Great Interview
notes.text:
Prepare before the conversation

Research the organisation, the role, recent work, and the interviewer when that information is public. Prepare a focused answer to 'Tell me about yourself' that lasts about 60 to 90 seconds. Connect your background to the role and finish with why the opportunity interests you. Prepare two or three genuine questions for the interviewer.

Use the STAR method

For behavioural questions, structure the answer as Situation, Task, Action, and Result. Set the context briefly, explain your responsibility, spend most of the time on the actions you personally took, and close with a measurable result or lesson. A college project, internship, volunteer role, or part-time job can provide strong examples. Aim for about two minutes.

Manage the interview well

Arrive ten to fifteen minutes early. For an online interview, test the link, internet connection, audio, camera, and lighting. Dress neatly, sit with an attentive posture, and listen to the complete question before answering. If you do not know something, be honest and explain how you would find out instead of inventing an answer.

Avoid common mistakes

Do not criticise a past employer, college, or colleague. Replace vague claims with examples, keep your phone away, and ask at least one thoughtful question. Confidence comes from preparation and clarity, not pretending to know everything.

notes.title: After the Interview
notes.text:
Follow up professionally

Send a short thank-you email within 24 hours of the interview. Keep it to three or four clear lines: thank the interviewer, mention one useful point from the conversation, restate your interest, and close politely. Personalising one detail shows attention without turning the email into another application.

If the employer gave a decision date, wait until that date has passed. If no timeline was shared, one polite follow-up after about a week is reasonable. Avoid repeated messages. A delayed reply does not always mean rejection, but professional boundaries still matter.

Read the whole offer

Review the salary, joining date, work location, notice period, probation terms, benefits, and any conditions. Ask questions about unclear language before accepting. It is reasonable to request a short period to decide, especially when you need to compare the role with other commitments.

Negotiate with evidence

Base a negotiation on reliable market research, the responsibilities of the role, and the value your experience can provide. Make a specific, courteous request rather than an ultimatum. Consider the full package, not only the headline salary.

Never pay a fee to obtain a job. Requests for recruitment payments, equipment deposits, or confidential banking information before normal verification can signal a scam. Verify the employer through official channels before sharing sensitive information or accepting an offer.
